item.title: Rich medieval Danes bought graves ‘closer to God’ despite leprosy stigma, archaeologists find
item.description: Study of inequality in medieval graves shows that stigmatized illnesses didn’t bar people from socially prestigious burials

item.title: Advancing research integrity in 2025: leading with action and impact
item.description: At Frontiers, research integrity and quality sit at the heart of everything we publish. Supporting this commitment is our dedicated Research Integrity team, working behind the scenes to safeguard the scientific record at scale. item.title: Frogs new to science and proof we’d rather look anywhere but at spiders: Here are Frontiers’ photo highlights of the month
item.description: At Frontiers, we bring some of the world’s best research to a global audience. But with tens of thousands of articles published each year, it’s impossible to see all that research in the same way scientists do. Here are some images that showcase some of the newest findings published in the last month.

item.title: Bacteria frozen in ancient underground ice cave found to be resistant against 10 modern antibiotics
item.description: A bacterial strain thriving in icy environments could sharpen antibiotic resistance crisis – or help solve it, new research shows

item.title: Brainwaves of mothers and children synchronize when playing together – even in an acquired language
item.description: Neural synchrony between mothers and children doesn’t require native language proficiency

item.title: Frontiers Women in Science – Five years on
item.description: Looking back at 2025, our fifth year publishing the Women in Science blog series, I feel an immense sense of pride in what we have achieved as a group. With 76 insightful articles published over the past five years, it is clear that women researchers continue to need a dedicated platform with readers who remain strongly engaged with their stories. item.title: Scientists reveal our best- and worst-case scenarios for a warming Antarctica
item.description: New study on the Antarctic Peninsula shows that the choices we make in the next decade will determine Antarctica’s fate for centuries

item.title: How bacteria can reclaim lost energy, nutrients, and clean water from wastewater
item.description: Wastewater contains untapped resources that, if reclaimed, could power agriculture, global sanitation, and its own treatment to help us meet UN SDG goals, according to a review published in Frontiers in Science.

item.title: Middle-aged men are most vulnerable to faster aging due to ‘forever chemicals’
item.description: Aging effect of specific PFAS is found to be greatest in men between 50 and 65

item.title: Celebrity dolphin of Venice doesn’t need special protection – except from humans
item.description: A dolphin returning to a historic habitat necessitates management of people, not wildlife, researchers monitoring solitary bottlenose dolphin in Venice say
